General.Description:
The kitchen on the Rue des Martyrs is small enough that two people cooking in it must negotiate every movement — who reaches for the salt, who stirs the pot, who stands at the window when the other needs the full length of the counter. For twenty-two years it was the kitchen Celine Dupont shared with her husband, Olivier. For the last three years, it has been hers alone.

A Kitchen in Paris is structured around the seasons of a single year, and within each season around the recipes that Celine cooked — some for the first time alone, some for the hundredth time, all of them differently charged with memory and loss and the complicated business of continuing to eat when someone you loved is no longer there to eat with.

It is, in part, a book about grief. But it is equally a book about food — about the specific intelligence of French home cooking, the patience required by a proper stock, the way that brioche dough, correctly made, feels like something living in your hands. Dupont writes about both with equal honesty and equal love.

The recipes included throughout are not supplementary. They are the text.

Extraordinarily beautiful. One of the most consoling books you will ever read.
